name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,630

clue.text: Share of party vote going west?

indicators.note: in an across entry, travelling west means reading from right to left, so the word runs backwards

blocks.note: a do is an informal word for a party or celebration
a poll is a vote or ballot

explanation.surface: A question about what fraction of a party's support is drifting rightward, or westward, in an election.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Share of party vote' reads as one political phrase, but 'Share' is the definition and only the vote is turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: A dollop is a lump or helping of something, so it can stand for a portion handed out to someone.

clue.text: Discourage careful eater, second to quit

indicators.note: the letter in position two is told to leave, so it is dropped from the word

blocks.note: someone on a diet watches carefully what they eat

explanation.surface: Advice to put off a fussy eater, with a second helping withdrawn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second' sounds like a second course; it means the second letter, the I of DIETER, which goes to leave DETER.
explanation.definitionFit: To deter someone is to put them off doing something, which is a plain synonym for discouraging them.

clue.text: Enthusiastic rally, regularly itch to get involved

indicators.note: at regular intervals means taking every other letter of the word
things that get involved become tangled together, so the letters are mixed up

blocks.note: taken as written
first and third letters of the word

explanation.surface: An excited crowd at a rally, with fidgety supporters itching to join in.
explanation.walkthrough: The two letters from 'itch' join the letters of 'rally', and all seven are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Waxing lyrical means speaking with great gushing praise, so lyrical describes effusive, eager feeling.

clue.text: Home let - tenant brings in food

indicators.note: the phrase brings something inside itself, so the word sits within the run of letters

blocks.note: the letters run across the three words once the dash and spaces are ignored

explanation.surface: A landlord's note: a house is let and the tenant pays rent, or brings in provisions.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer spans 'hOME LET TEnant', ignoring the dash; 'food' is the definition at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: An omelette is a dish of beaten eggs cooked in a pan, a particular example of something you eat.

clue.text: Some lass! A man thanks her

indicators.note: only part of the following words is wanted, a portion of the letters

blocks.note: the letters run from the end of the first word into the start of the last

explanation.surface: An admiring exclamation about a fine girl, whom a man then thanks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some lass!' reads as praise, but 'Some' is the signal; the name sits in 'laSS A MAN THAnks', and 'her' is the vague definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Samantha is a woman's first name, so any woman called that can be referred to by the pronoun.

clue.text: Ship carrying computer equipment and beer going north supplying islands

indicators.note: a vessel carrying cargo holds it inside, so one word goes inside another
in a down entry, travelling north means reading upward, so the word is turned round

blocks.note: the Argo was the ship of Jason and the Argonauts in Greek myth
a silicon chip is a computer component
ale is a kind of beer

explanation.surface: A cargo ship heading north with computers and beer to supply a group of islands.
explanation.walkthrough: The ship is the classical Argo, not a generic vessel; it holds the chip and the upturned ale.
explanation.definitionFit: An archipelago is a cluster or chain of isles in a sea, so the plural noun names it well.

clue.text: Out-and-out guarantee leader’s been ousted

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter, and ousting it removes that letter

blocks.note: a warranty or warrant is a guarantee

explanation.surface: A complete promise that a political leader has been thrown out.
explanation.walkthrough: Dropping the W from WARRANT leaves the answer; 'leader' looks political but means the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Arrant means utter or complete, as in arrant nonsense, matching the adjective meaning thoroughgoing.

clue.text: Enter four or six in test? Of little importance

indicators.note: to enter is to go into something, so these letters are put inside another word

blocks.note: Roman numeral for four; the six, VI, works equally well
a trial is a test

explanation.surface: A cricketer hitting a boundary for four or six in a Test match, then shrugging it off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Four or six' sounds like cricket scoring; either Roman numeral fits the gap in the test, landing on the same letters, which is why the setter can offer both.
explanation.definitionFit: Trivial things are minor and unimportant, so the adjective matches the phrase about small significance.

clue.text: Lacking cover, relative introduces a bizarre rule

indicators.note: to introduce something is to put it in, so one piece goes inside the other
something bizarre is strange and out of shape, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: an aunt is a relative
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An eccentric aunt bringing in a strange rule that nobody need wear clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'introduces' means the relative takes the A inside her, just before her last letter, with the jumbled rule tacked on after.
explanation.definitionFit: Au naturel is French for in the natural state, used in English to mean naked or unclothed.

clue.text: Times covering row - with United missing goal

indicators.note: a cover goes around what it covers, so outer letters enclose the rest
something missing is absent, so those letters are left out

blocks.note: T is the abbreviation for time, so two times are T and T
to row is to quarrel or argue
U is the standard abbreviation for United in team names

explanation.surface: A newspaper report on a football row, with Manchester United failing to score.
explanation.walkthrough: The italics make 'Times' look like the newspaper; it is simply two Ts, holding ARGUE with its U removed.
explanation.definitionFit: A target is an aim or objective you work toward, a direct synonym for goal.

clue.text: Arachnid is on crop unfortunately

indicators.note: an unfortunate outcome is one that went wrong, so the letters come out disordered

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A farmer's bad news: a spider-like creature has been found on the harvest.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition comes first; the three short words supply exactly eight letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A scorpion belongs to the class of eight-legged creatures that includes spiders, mites and ticks.

clue.text: Expert sorts nice ticket for play

indicators.note: letters put into play are free to move around and take new positions

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A knowledgeable person arranges a good ticket for a theatre show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sorts' looks like the verb of the surface, but it is part of the fodder; 'play' is the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A rocket scientist is the stock idiom for a very clever person, as in 'it doesn't take one'.

clue.text: As chambermaid might for computer program

blocks.note: surface: describing what a hotel maid does when making a bed
setter's reading: that bed-making action, put as two words, is also the name of software for tables of figures

explanation.surface: A hotel maid's routine likened to some piece of software.
explanation.walkthrough: A chambermaid making beds would spread a sheet; joined up, that phrase is the program.
explanation.definitionFit: A spreadsheet is application software arranging numbers in rows and columns for calculation.

clue.text: Frankly discuss seasonal meal?

blocks.note: first meaning: the idiom for speaking bluntly and getting down to business
second meaning, taken literally: chatting about the bird eaten at Christmas

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the playful literal reading: the turkey is the Christmas dinner centrepiece.
explanation.definitionFit: To talk turkey is an idiom meaning to speak plainly about practical matters, especially in negotiation.

clue.text: He’s up with what’s new, distributing top titles

indicators.note: distributing spreads things out into new places, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A trendy publisher who keeps up with fashion and hands out bestsellers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up with what's new' sounds like being fashionable; here 'up' means airborne in a new aircraft.
explanation.definitionFit: A test pilot flies newly built aircraft to check them, so he is literally aloft in new machines.

clue.text: Smear, brutal, unfair - extremely

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its two ends, so only those letters are kept

blocks.note: first and last letters
first and last letters

explanation.surface: A complaint that a smear campaign was savage and deeply unjust.
explanation.walkthrough: 'extremely' looks like an intensifier for 'unfair'; it applies to both words before it.
explanation.definitionFit: To smear something makes it indistinct, and a blur is a smudged, unclear mark or image.

clue.text: Flab lost exercising in US game?

indicators.note: exercising works things over and moves them about, so the letters are put in motion

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone shedding weight by playing an American sport.
explanation.walkthrough: 'US game' is the definition, with the question mark nodding at the surface's weight-loss story.
explanation.definitionFit: Softball is a variant of baseball with a larger ball, widely played across America.

clue.text: Dress is taken back over a rip primarily

indicators.note: taking something back returns it the way it came, so the letters run backwards
primarily means in the first place, so only the opening letter is used
one thing laid over another can cover it on both sides, wrapping around it

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
first letter

explanation.surface: A dress returned to the shop because it has a tear.
explanation.walkthrough: IS turned round gives SI, which goes around A and the first letter of 'rip'.
explanation.definitionFit: A sari is a long draped garment worn by women in South Asia, a kind of dress.

clue.text: Wine selection from clarets in Athens

indicators.note: a selection from something is a part of it, so the word sits inside the letters that follow

blocks.note: the letters run across the three words

explanation.surface: A wine list in a Greek restaurant offering a choice of red Bordeaux.
explanation.walkthrough: Hidden in 'claRETS IN Athens'; the Greek setting is a fair hint, since the answer is a Greek wine.
explanation.definitionFit: Retsina is a Greek white or rosé flavoured with pine resin, a particular kind of vino.

clue.text: Both sides upset with Panorama? Hard to explain

indicators.note: something upset is knocked over and disturbed, so the letters fall into a new order

blocks.note: left and right are L and R
taken as written

explanation.surface: Politicians from both sides angry at a TV documentary; Panorama is the BBC's long-running investigative programme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Both sides' reads as political parties; it gives L and R, which join the eight letters of the programme name.
explanation.definitionFit: Paranormal events lie beyond normal scientific understanding, so they resist rational explanation.

clue.text: House island boy, first person to be admitted

indicators.note: someone admitted is let inside, so this letter goes into the word

blocks.note: the Isle of Man, in the Irish Sea
a son is a boy
I is the first person singular pronoun

explanation.surface: A grand house on an island where a boy is the first to be let in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'first person' sounds like whoever arrives first; it is the grammatical first person.
explanation.definitionFit: A mansion is a large and stately dwelling, a grand kind of residence.

clue.text: Last stop - overlooking Northern River

indicators.note: in a down entry, one thing overlooking another sits above it, setting the order

blocks.note: to stop is to end
the Ure is a river in North Yorkshire

explanation.surface: The final halt on a route, with a view across a river in the North.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Last stop' reads as one phrase, but 'Last' is the verb definition and 'overlooking' means placed above.
explanation.definitionFit: To last is to go on or survive over time, and to endure has exactly that verbal sense.

clue.text: Do wrong in lowdown way?

blocks.note: surface: making a mistake, perhaps sneakily
setter's reading: 'lowdown' means near the ground, where the body part used for walking is, so the blunder is made with that part

explanation.walkthrough: 'lowdown' suggests something mean or underhand; the joke is that the offending body part is the lowest one.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to make an embarrassing tactless blunder, a social error rather than a crime.

clue.text: Casks I observed inside port

indicators.note: to be seen inside something is to be within it, so one piece sits in another

blocks.note: large barrels for wine or beer, plural
taken as written

explanation.surface: A customs officer reporting barrels spotted in a harbour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I observed' reads as the speaker witnessing; I is the letter that goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Tunis is the capital of Tunisia, a city with a harbour on the Mediterranean coast.

clue.text: Was first to go around India certainly not needing to work

indicators.note: going around something encircles it, so the outer word wraps the inner letters

blocks.note: to be first, at the front, is to have led
India is I in the NATO phonetic alphabet
'sure' is an informal way of saying certainly

explanation.surface: A wealthy traveller who was first to tour India and never had to earn a living.
explanation.walkthrough: 'go around India' suggests travel; here the past tense of lead encloses I and SURE.
explanation.definitionFit: The leisured classes have ample free time, living on private means without having to earn wages.

clue.text: Excellent upright character with article favouring gradual change

blocks.note: fab is short for fabulous
the letter I is a single vertical stroke
an is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: Praise for an honest person who writes a piece advocating slow reform.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upright character' sounds like an honest person; it is the letter shaped like a vertical line.
explanation.definitionFit: The Fabian Society, a British socialist group, advocates reform by slow steps rather than revolution.

clue.text: Cross about ultimately bitter Bible parody

indicators.note: about means around, so the outer word encircles the others
ultimately means in the end, so the final letter is the one kept

blocks.note: cross and testy both mean irritable
last letter
AV is the Authorised Version of the Bible

explanation.surface: An angry believer furious about a mocking spoof of scripture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cross' could suggest a crucifix in a Bible surface; it means bad-tempered.
explanation.definitionFit: A travesty is a grotesque or absurd imitation of something, a mocking version like a parody.

clue.text: Kinnock maybe good Labour leader? Electorate not yet sure, for a start

indicators.note: the leader of a word is the letter at its front
the start of each word is its opening letter, so only that is kept

blocks.note: G is the abbreviation for good
first letter
first letters of the four words

explanation.surface: Was Kinnock a good Labour leader? Voters still undecided at the outset; Neil Kinnock led Britain's Labour Party in the 1980s.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface points to Neil Kinnock, but 'maybe' signals an example: his wife, also a Labour politician.
explanation.definitionFit: Glenys Kinnock was a Labour MEP and minister, so she is one person bearing that surname.
